content: Uranium carbonates exhibit a unique solubility behavior in water compared to most other carbonates. While the majority of carbonates are insoluble in water, uranium carbonates are often soluble. This is attributed to the ability of the uranium(VI) cation (U(VI)) to bind with two terminal oxides and three or more carbonate ions, forming anionic complexes. Fraction diagrams illustrate that as the pH of a uranium(VI) solution increases, uranium transitions into hydrated uranium oxide hydroxide and, at even higher pH levels, into an anionic hydroxide complex. When carbonate is introduced to the system, uranium forms a series of carbonate complexes as the pH rises. These reactions significantly enhance uranium solubility in the pH range of 6 to 8, which is a critical consideration for the long-term stability of spent uranium dioxide nuclear fuels. When uranium metal is heated to temperatures between 250°C and 300°C (482°F to 572°F), it reacts with hydrogen to form uranium hydride. At even higher temperatures, the hydrogen can be reversibly removed. This property makes uranium hydrides useful as starting materials for producing reactive uranium powders, as well as various uranium carbide, nitride, and halide compounds. Uranium hydride exists in two crystalline forms: the α form, which is obtained at lower temperatures, and the β form, which forms above 250°C. Uranium carbides and uranium nitrides are semimetallic compounds that are relatively inert, minimally soluble in acids, reactive with water, and capable of igniting in air to form U₃O₈. Uranium carbides include uranium monocarbide (UC), uranium dicarbide (UC₂), and diuranium tricarbide (U₂C₃). UC and UC₂ are produced by adding carbon to molten uranium or exposing uranium to carbon monoxide at high temperatures. U₂C₃, stable below 1800°C, is prepared by applying mechanical stress to a heated mixture of UC and UC₂. Uranium nitrides, such as uranium mononitride (UN), uranium dinitride (UN₂), and diuranium trinitride (U₂N₃), are formed by directly exposing uranium metal to nitrogen. All uranium fluorides are derived from uranium tetrafluoride (UF₄), which is prepared by hydrofluorination of uranium dioxide. Reduction of UF₄ with hydrogen at 1000°C produces uranium trifluoride (UF₃). Under specific temperature and pressure conditions, solid UF₄ reacts with gaseous uranium hexafluoride (UF₆) to form intermediate fluorides such as U₂F₉, U₄F₁₇, and UF₅. UF₆, a white solid with high vapor pressure at room temperature, is highly reactive and easily sublimates, making it essential for the gaseous diffusion process used to separate uranium-235 from uranium-238. UF₆ is prepared from uranium dioxide and uranium hydride through the following reactions: 1. UO₂ + 4HF + heat (500°C) → UF₄ + 2H₂O 2. UF₄ + F₂ + heat (350°C) → UF₆ The resulting UF₆ is the most volatile uranium compound known, with significant utility in isotope separation. Uranium tetrachloride (UCl₄) can be prepared by directly combining chlorine with uranium metal or uranium hydride. Reduction of UCl₄ with hydrogen yields uranium trichloride (UCl₃), while higher uranium chlorides are formed by reaction with additional chlorine. All uranium chlorides react with water and air. Uranium bromides and iodides, such as UBr₃, UBr₄, UI₃, and UI₄, are formed by reacting uranium with bromine or iodine, or by adding uranium hydride (UH₃) to the respective acids. Uranium oxyhalides, including UO₂F₂, UOCl₂, UO₂Cl₂, and UO₂Br₂, are water-soluble, with their stability decreasing as the atomic weight of the halide increases. Uranium-238 is an alpha emitter that decays through an 18-member natural decay series, ultimately forming lead-206. Uranium-235, also known as actino-uranium, undergoes a 15-member decay series ending in lead-207, with intermediate isotopes such as protactinium-231 and actinium-227. The consistent decay rates in these series allow for radiometric dating by comparing parent-to-daughter element ratios. Uranium-233 is produced from thorium-232 via neutron bombardment. Uranium-235 is critical for nuclear reactors and weapons because it is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope, capable of sustaining a chain reaction with thermal neutrons. Uranium-238, while not fissile, is important for absorbing neutrons to produce plutonium-239, another fissile isotope. Enrichment of uranium ore through isotope separation is necessary to concentrate uranium-235 for use in nuclear weapons and most nuclear power plants, except for pressurized heavy water reactors. A critical mass of uranium-235 is required to sustain a nuclear chain reaction. Enriched uranium typically contains 3-5% uranium-235, significantly higher than its natural abundance. The enrichment process generates large quantities of depleted uranium (DU), which has a reduced uranium-235 concentration and an increased uranium-238 fraction. Depleted uranium is defined as having a uranium-235 concentration significantly lower than its natural level. In recent years, depleted uranium hexafluoride stores have gained value, with prices rising from $5 per kilogram in 2001 to over $130 per kilogram in July 2007, as re-enrichment of DU with 0.3-0.35% uranium-235 is being considered.
